utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today is Tuesday, the 15th of January, 2008. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, as well as the accused. We must resume yesterday's hearing and bring in the witness into the courtroom. In the meantime, I have an oral decision to hand down. I would like the registrar to move into private session for a few moments, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to inform the parties that the registrar has just raised a technical issue which I am discovering, but this requires additional information. It seems that if one of you discusses a topic in private session we have to stop for 30 minutes to enable the technician to do what's required. So I'm very surprised by what I've just been told but this is what the registrar has just told me. So if you'd like to move into private session, please think twice about it, because we would then have to have a 30-minute break. Mr. Prlic, I believe you would like to have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I need to say what I have to say in open session, and I would indeed prefer the whole trial to be held in open session, and this is the essence of my brief request: The Trial Chamber decided yesterday to punish or sanction my Defence counsel, preventing him from actively defending me in the courtroom for a certain period of time and it was done in open session. Bearing in mind that both interventions of may lawyer that led to this response on the part of the Trial Chamber were actually done in private session, both in the cross-examination -- in the course of the cross-examination and in his address to the Trial Chamber. This was all done in closed session. So I believe that it would be a good idea and I believe that the Trial Chamber will support me on this in order to make this trial transparent. So I think it would be a good idea to make it possible for those two interventions on the part of my lawyer to be accessible to public. In light of the fact that this witness testified in closed session, perhaps some elements might be redacted, some words might be redacted, if such words might lead to the identification of the witness who testified in this courtroom over the past two weeks. So it is my request to make public the two interventions of my lawyer that led to this decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have been seized of your applications, and we'll deliberate on the matter you've just raised. We shall now bring in the witness into the courtroom. I'll give the floor to the registrar in the meantime so that we can have some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution response to exhibits tendered by Prlic Defence for Witness BF will become Exhibit IC 773. Prosecution response to exhibits tendered by Stojic Defence for Witness BF will become Exhibit IC 774. Prosecution response to exhibits tendered by Praljak Defence for Witness BF will become Exhibit IC 775, and Prosecution response to exhibits tendered by Petkovic Defence for Witness BF will become Exhibit IC 776.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not receiving any interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the timing is concerned, let me repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lead counsel had 40 minutes yesterday. You therefore have 26 minutes left unless the other Defence counsel have given you some of their time, which I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Witness, and good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. The Prlic Defence has no further questions for this witness and we cede our time to Mr. Stojic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir. We are going to resume your cross-examination. Prlic's Defence counsel has just told us that they have no further questions for you. Their time has been given to the Defence counsel of Mr. Stojic. I shall now give the floor to the counsel who would like to take the floor. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. As far as I can see the Trial Chamber has just been given the exhibits that I intend to use, and I could please ask the usher to give the exhibits that I intend to use to the witness and to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as you have just heard, I have been given the time that remained to the Prlic Defence for my cross-examination, but I don't think that I will be using up all of this time. I think that I will be able to complete the cross-examination in the time that I was allotted originally, but I will try to do that as slowly as possible so that we can avoid any interventions to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, before you left Mostar on the 1st of September, 1993, you arranged the evacuation of the wounded from the hospital in East Mostar and the hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The meeting where all the details were supposed to be arranged was held in Medjugorje on the 1st of September, 1993, and you attended that meeting. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it immediately in my memory. Perhaps I might just say that when the political decisions had been taken to create a system of removal with their consent of the various persons who had been injured or sick, once that had been taken, fundamentally it was left up to other colleagues, perhaps more junior, and I myself was not very much involved. In immediate answer to your question, however, I hope that you -- that you feel that this is an appropriate way to approach it, I think it's -- I cannot remember whether I was present at that meeting or not. There was a host of meetings because there were problems -- problems all the way with that system of removal of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But if I understand you correctly, you've just told us, in addition to the answer to my question, that this was part of a process, indicating that it lasted over a period of several days and that in the end the -- there was this evacuation. Could you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a partial evacuation. The evacuation, as I recall it, and it wasn't fully sent through to me, they didn't -- they didn't tell me all the detail of it, the -- yes, the -- the -- the issue came -- was sent to -- was kicked upstairs, as they say, and we had to deal with the political aspects, and those tended to hang around maybe for at least six weeks. They were being recorded and sent to -- usually to Stoltenberg in -- in -- sorry. They were sent to Stoltenberg in Zagreb or wherever he was at that time. He wasn't at that meeting either. We left it, as I said, mostly to our subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, I would like to focus on this evacuation that was arranged, the one that you managed to agree on, and let me now show you a document that might refresh your memory about some details.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher please assist the witness with the first document in my binder. That's document P 4857. Just so that the witness familiarise himself with the methods that we use here. The first document I want him to look at is P 4857. That's the first green sticker on my binder. I think that we have the translation in the original here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, this is a report from the first meeting held on the 1st of September, 1993. It is signed by the chief of the inspection service in the HVO, Mr. Ivo Sandrk, a man who apparently attended this meeting, and I would now like us to go very briefly through some of the details. You can see here that he's talking about the 1st of September 1993, listing the names of the people who were present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, in the document I can see the name of a witness who has been granted protective measures, so please avoid mentioning the name of that witness so that we are not faced with the technical problem I mentioned earlier on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. Thank you. Thank you. Yes, I've seen that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Anyway, can you look at the middle of the page or, rather, your name is mentioned here, too, saying that you were present at the meeting. Could you take a look at that? Can you see that portion? I'll give you some time to find it. Do you remember that on the 1st of September you did indeed attend that meeting and that in fact after that meeting you left straight away? So that's the last day according to your reports.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's the day that I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, we said it was an ongoing process and we see on page 2 and the other date, the 2nd of September, which means that the meetings continued at 1000 hours on the 2nd of September and at this meeting the technical details were agreed upon with respect to the evacuation, the conditions that each party was to meet, and it was agreed that they should ensure the resources necessary to carry out the evacuation, the final destination where the wounded are to be evacuated to. Mr. Thornberry, do you remember that this is how the process continued? Can you remember this detail, that each party was supposed to secure the necessary means of evacuation?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you mean -- when you say the means of evacuation, I take it you are not referring to whether it is by land or by air or -- how is that intended, please, that question, that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From the document further on we can see that it was necessary to ensure helicopters for this, but I'm just asking you whether you remember that part of the negotiations incorporated the preparations that I read out, that is to say the term I used, "to ensure resources for the evacuation." If you can't remember that, we can move on. It's not a particularly important detail, but I just want to check out and see which information you had about how the evacuation ensued after you had left Mostar and Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't at all want to convey a contrary feeling, but I would have to say that it would be very unlikely for this kind of detail to be brought to me other than for a formal signature, and I cannot remember going behind that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I do apologise. Now all my questions linked to this document -- well, if you feel that some information from this document wasn't essential as far as you were concerned, essential that you know about them, but I should like to continue along those lines. And now, on the 3rd of September, and you'll find that on page 3, the -- was the third day of the negotiations, and the meeting started in Medjugorje once again at 1000 hours, and from this paragraph and this section related to the third day and the 3rd of September, it says that the Muslim side did not have the helicopters ready for the evacuation, so that the entire operation, well, was not brought into question but was delayed for those reasons. It had to be postponed. So can you remember anything about that, because it was, after all, a significant operation both for your mission and for the sick people and for the evacuation of persons from Nova Bila and East Mostar and so on. So did you receive information to that effect, that they did come across these difficulties, the difficulties that I've just described to you briefly?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they came across not only those difficulties but a number of others which were more political than technical. But as I tried to suggest a little earlier, in principle this kind of paper doesn't come to me. Except, of course, as you have -- as madam has indicated, except as regards as the -- the kinds of question which crossed boundaries, as it were, in -- in a supervision of this kind of process. It was an extremely difficult process, because the parties had been fighting each other for a long time and they hadn't got used to the idea that maybe they could do things some other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, you have helped me a great deal with that answer of yours when you said that it wasn't just these technical details that were a problem but that there were a series of problems, and you mentioned political goodwill. So that's why I'm showing you this document, which I'm sure didn't reach you because it's an HVO document. So I'm not actually asking you about the document but about the information contained therein, and I just wanted to indicate that political and military aspect of this whole operation and the operation of transporting the -- the wounded later on. And I'd like to indicate just one more detail to see if you were informed about that. If we carry on through this document and look at the 3rd of September once again, it says that the Muslim side did finally secure helicopters. And I'm going to read a sentence out to you slowly, and it says: "And the evacuation was to have begun on the 3rd of September at 1500 hours from the plateau or open area by the former bus station." And then the following information is provided: It says at 1400 hours -- at 1430 hours rather, there was a mortar attack by the MOS forces on part of the town under HVO control. On that occasion 18 civilians were wounded of which five were children -- five civilians were killed, two of them children. Among the wounded civilians there were eight Muslims." Now, you see when the departure of 1500 hours was decided upon, then the HVO, and this is what it says in the document, "... cautioned UNPROFOR representatives," and told them that "... incidents could be expected on the MOS side, MOS forces side, in order to show that the HVO was trying to obstruct the agreement." Now, any of these details here which would come under military and political details but important to see whether your agreement was obstructed, have you ever seen this information before?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have an extremely vague memory of something coming up and having to be dealt with on an emergency basis, but I'm sorry to say my memory does not run -- at this stage does not run further than that. I wish it did, but I can't do that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From this document, just to finish my questions on that, so that part of the evacuation that was agreed was completed on the 6th of September, 1993; is that right? Now, from this entire document it would follow and emerge that the representatives on the Muslim side changed every time. Different people attended the negotiations every time. So what I'm going to ask you is this: In your statement, Mr. Thornberry, you said that -- you said this in court and also in the written statement you gave to the Prosecutor, that you encountered a very serious and difficult situation and difficult conditions in East Mostar. Now, Mr. Thornberry, at that time, and linked to these negotiations and we've just shown one document about them or later on linked to negotiations which took place later as you said almost six weeks later, did you gain the impression that the BH army, as concerns the wounded, was using the wounded in order to further its military and political goals, to achieve them? Did you gain that impression?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did, I don't remember its specifics. And if I did, it's very likely that not only the BH army but others were using the wounded at that time. When I say using it, I don't mean in some Machiavellian way but, rather, in a manner which will -- which would -- which would enable them to fall back on some expedient if they found that the situation was becoming unacceptable for them because of their political -- the political commitment which they might have made. In other words, the -- the BH army was really doing what I think most people do after a very major conflict and they have something pressed on them of a humanitarian nature, they -- they tend to be cautious in how they accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, before you continue your questions, as regards the technical issue I mentioned a moment ago, here is the situation: Everything that is being said is live. As you know, usually we have a 30-minute delay in the broadcast. For an unknown reason, everything we're saying today is broadcast live, which means that if somebody mentions the name of a protected witness or a confidential event, there will be no possibility for us to redact the transcript, because as said, everything is broadcast live. Our technicians are trying to solve the problem, but for the time being it hasn't been. So please be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for that warning. I'll do my best. And I think in the questions that I have prepared, there is not a single document which could be of the nature which you have just described.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, your answer was that all the sides tried to use the wounded. Now, the Trial Chamber here must gain the right impression, must gain an insight as to what the real conditions were when it came to the HVO and children and civilians. So a precise picture is what is needed. And which of those conditions either of the parties was able to wield influence on. Now, I'd like us to continue this topic for us to see whether the BH army accepted the solutions offered up by the international agencies and organisations or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, we have a document, a document that's been shown to you by the Defence. As of the 3rd of September, obviously there has been discussions between the HVO and the BH army on the issue of the evacuation of the wounded. All of this, of course, was done with the international community having been informed. And suddenly - that's what the document shows, at least - the Muslim side attacks. An attack is carried out, and at 2.30 p.m. to be more specific. Attack with mortar. According to that document, 18 civilians were wounded. Among them five were children. Five civilians were killed, and among those five killed there were also two children. So two children were killed, and five were wounded. One could believe that since the BH army is attacking the HVO, all the victims are Croats. In fact, that's not what the document says, because among the victims there are also eight Muslim civilians. So it is quite surprising negotiations are going on, and then suddenly in the middle of those negotiations one of the parties decides to launch an attack. You were there at the time. Do you have yourself have an explanation to give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am afraid not, Mr. President. I don't have an explanation. Much that happened in the country at that time was without -- objectively without explanation. It seemed to be an attack upon the foundations of the agreement. But if I might just add this: From personal experience in regard to, for example, the situation in Sarajevo, when I negotiated there with the Serbs, the answers had been given by the Serbs to my questions were punctuated, I think is the word, by mortar shells which fell 20 metres away. And that was a mortar which was in fact Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic who were actually conducting that negotiation. So all I can say is, yes, I concede that -- that the circumstances were rather bizarre, and worse than that, obviously, horrible, but I'm afraid I can't put myself in the place of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you say that circumstances were bizarre. The question that comes to mind and to the Judge's mind in particular is the following: Were there individuals that behind the back of the official negotiators were playing an entirely different score? Were they not trying to sabotage the agreement being negotiated, or maybe they were pursuing other more mysterious goals? Did you have the feeling at any stage that there could be external individuals other than the negotiators themselves who would come there to sabotage the work that was being done? That's what -- I'm asking you because yesterday I was very impressed by the video that was shown to us, the video in which you met HVO officials, and I thought I recognised at some stage General Petkovic. And when one sees this video, one feels the climate, this almost fraternal climate, this atmosphere that comes out of such meetings between international representatives and HVO. The atmosphere is very friendly, as we saw yesterday in the video. So this question comes to mind: There are negotiations. Everybody is taking part in such negotiations, and then those attacks take place and they come and disrupt the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I have worked in peacekeeping for nearly 20 years, and in maybe half a dozen examples, and I do not know the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, we're going to continue discussing the medical evacuations. Now, I started my question a moment ago, so I'll repeat it now. From the documents that I wish to present to you, what I want to see is whether the BH army, if it was, and you say it was, and I have no reason to doubt that, if it was in such a difficult situation with respect to the wounded, then did it use everything possible to help its people and its own wounded? Now, do you remember whether after this evacuation that we're discussing, that is the evacuation of the 1st of September, the HVO made suggestions and proposals to the BH army about the evacuation of the wounded, especially women and children, from the hospital in East Mostar to the war hospital in West Mostar? Do you remember what the response was from the BH army when that request was made? And we're talking about the proposals and offers after this evacuation of the 1st -- from the 1st to the 6th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I -- I think that I do not have any memory of this aspect of a very complicated negotiation and delivery of personnel, wounded personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's take a look at another document in my binder. It is, in fact, the last green document. P 05428. With the green sticker. The last document. You've found it, I see.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the English version.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You will see that this is a report sent by the UN military observers to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The date is the 27th of September, 1993. It is a daily report for that particular day. And would you turn to page 5 of the English version and look at paragraph 4 on page 5. It's a long report, but I'm interested in paragraph 4 on page 5, which is page 6 of the Croatian text. And there on page 5, if you've found it, you will see paragraph 4, and there it talks about the continuation of the endeavours to help the wounded from the hospital, and it says: "Meetings. East Mostar had routine meeting with 4th Corps." It says: "Higher military observer met with General Pasalic." It is General Pasalic, in fact, because in brackets it says "Commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army." "... discussed his recent refusal to negotiate with the HVO while they continue shelling civilian targets. Discussions went on to the wish for peace. Of course the obvious conflict between the two points was highlighted." Now, the next portion is very important. "The HVO -- medical evacuation for women and children to the west hospital has been offered by the HVO. However, it would appear that the Bosnian-Herzegovinian side is unlikely to take advantage of this due to the political advantage that such an arrangement or evacuation would give the HVO." Can you remember discussions of this kind and refusal on the part of the BH army with respect to the evacuation of civilians? Perhaps it would be a good idea to take a look at another document first, sir, which you may have seen yourself. The document is 2D 455. And that might be the proposal by the HVO. It's the second document in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher help us out. The document number is 2D 455.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a document --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: -- which -- it's an HVO signed by the assistant chief of medical health care department, Mr. Ivan Bagaric. It is dated the 16th of September 1993, and I'd just like to mention that a moment ago we read a report dated the 27th of September. Now, in this document sent both to UNPROFOR and the Spanish Battalion, Mr. Bagaric is issuing a request to help the Muslim side -- to offer the Muslim side the accommodation and hospitalisation of civilians, especially women and children in the Mostar war hospital as well as other HVO hospitals. Mr. Bagaric also says that the sick and wounded -- Muslim sick and wounded would be guaranteed the same treatment as our civilians, and he says, "We propose that the control of our work could be done by the International Red Cross, the European or, rather, EC monitors and UNPROFOR." And he goes on it to say that: "We are doing this for only one reason. It is the humanitarian reason. Therefore, we kindly ask you not to make any political connotations to this matter." So this is quite obviously related to the offer conveyed through the UN monitors to the east side and Mr. Pasalic. Can you remember anything linked to this type of situation?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a -- there were steps towards a cease-fire and agreement about that, to achieve that, from as early as late -- late July. From that time on, the basic concern of the parties -- I want to qualify this in just a moment. Basic concern of the parties was to advance their position in respect of a potential settlement, especially in regard to land, territory. The qualification I want to make is that of course that isn't a consistent pattern. It didn't happen all the time. And beyond that, I'm sorry, I cannot go. There were very complicated cross-curtains -- cross-currents there, and I am not really able to decipher them for you. I wish I could, but I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, do you have information according to which the HVO offered the BH army medicines previously, prior to that, and that part of that the BH army accepted, that it also offered to transport the wounded to the war hospital in West Mostar and further on to Croatia, and that was partially done? And do you know that the HVO, even before these events, offered the BH army the joint use of one of the hospitals in West Mostar in which all the wounded would be put up together and who would be treated by the same doctors, both Muslims and Croats, and which would be secured by UNPROFOR? Now, Mr. Thornberry, I don't want to make it difficult for you in anyway. You say you don't remember many of the details, but try and tell me the things that you do remember. And I'm asking you this for the simple reason to see who actually cared for the wounded and civilians and to what extent, but I am focusing now -- or, rather, I know that you had far greater problems to deal with with respect to taking in humanitarian aid, to bringing a stop to the hostilities and so on and so forth, but I am always very sensitive when it comes to the wounded, especially women, children, and anyone who was sick. So what I'm asking you now is do you know that the HVO made every effort even before this to resolve this question in the best possible way, or in a better way than it had been resolved and then the conditions were at the hospital in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would certainly not have been possible for them to have been worse. But that much said, I -- I'm really in a quandary about this, because I know, and I'm sure you can tell me, madam, something of what was going on behind the scenes. Not merely on the humanitarian but also on the political side. I've tried to suggest that, as I'm sure, madam, you are well aware, not everything seemed to be so actually was. This is the difficulty which -- one of the difficulties that I faced at the moment. I wish I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you for your answer. I -- let me just make this clear to you. I thought that this document spoke for itself, the UN military observer's document, which indicates that assistance to evacuate the wounded was offered and the BH army rejected the offer saying that the HVO would thus gain political points, so I am rather confused not just you. But I'm using documents that you should have been or could have been familiar with, and you have great experience, so that's the reason why I am asking you all these questions. Let me just indicate for the transcript because I am afraid, I think that I am right, the that document speaking about the HVO offer to provide accommodation for the Muslim civilians and the BH army personnel and the Croat civilians and the HVO personnel in a Mostar hospital, a joint hospital, it's described in P 02923. I think this document is under seal. It is in my binder, but I don't want to show it to the witness because the witness itself -- well, in light of his answers. Finally, sir, on this topic, from all those documents that were shown to you, don't they show that the BH army was not ready -- or, rather, did not want for political or military reasons to accept even those solutions that were offered to it to alleviate the suffering of the wounded and the sick in the hospital in East Mostar in the period that is indicated in those documents? Could you please just tell me what is your impression, even if this is the first time that you see or hear of these official documents.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, what is the question therefore?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The question is based on your experience or the documents that you've just seen, does it not follow, irrefutably, that the BH army refused to accept the solutions that were placed at its disposal to help the wounded in the East Mostar hospital? And according to Mr. Pasalic's statement, it is quite apparent that it did not do so. It chose not to do so for military or political reasons.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a further reason, which is everybody was getting paranoid, and it was very difficult for those of us who were trying to act at least as some kind of brokers to persuade both sides that -- to -- to persuade them that we were, in fact, in good faith. But when the United Nations also is challenged and it's good faith is challenged, the situation becomes a bit more difficult still. And I'm sorry, madam, I would like to be able to answer your question more succinctly. I wish it were the case that there are black and white hatted cowboys, but there are not. We don't have clear indications here. I don't want to confuse the matter further, so I'd better not continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. You're giving me true political answers, and I fully understand -- understand them, but you did answer my question. There is another reason, if I understand you correctly. Therefore, you do agree that the reasons that I was talking about were also in play: The deliberate decision not to accept what was offered for political or military reasons.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. In the end let me just ask you to look at yet another document. This one is the document that you yourself drafted, and it will be easy for you to do so, but Judge Antonetti asked you yesterday about some high-ranking persons that you met in the course of your mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you recall whether you met at any time with Mr. Ejup Ganic? Do you remember who he was, and can you very briefly share your impressions of that man with us?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet Ejup Ganic. I met him several times. I did not meet him in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I met him in -- I met him in -- in -- let me think. I think it was actually in -- in the city. I think it was -- sorry, the word is gone for one silly moment. He was one of the people whom I consulted when I negotiated the air and -- airfield.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- and Ganic was the person on the Croat side whom it was my responsibility to interview and, if possible, to get on board for an agreement to share the airfield. I would -- I would not want to -- to make an evaluation of Mr. Ganic. He was a very shrewd political operator who sometimes provoked positive reactions and sometimes did not. I found him moderately difficult to do business with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, but let me just check. I think that on page 26, line 20, you said that Mr. Ganic was a representative of the Croat side. Is that what you meant or did you make a mistake?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whom he represented, in fact. There were times when it was very difficult to follow his activities. He -- he tended to focus in -- essentially in the -- in regard to events in the airfield matters, in the headquarters, these kinds of matters, rather than a field operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I think that your own report will serve to remind you whose side -- which side he represented. Let us look at the fourth document in my binder. The number is P 4395.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I go back to Ganic? I'd forgotten that I hadn't given the answer to you on that one. Mr. Ganic was one of my interlocutors in the main city, and I dealt with him in regard to major questions of policy. He was very close to Mr. Izetbegovic. In fact, he was really the major figure with Mr. Izetbegovic until late July of 1993. Around about late July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Thornberry, we can agree that he did not represent the Croat side but, as you just indicated, the Muslim or the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] The usher is right next to you to assist you. I asked for document P 04395?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to assist the witness in finding the English version and so that he can identify this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This, sir, is a document that you yourself forwarded. This is your report. The date is the 22nd of August, 1993. Could we please look at page 3 in the English version. That would correspond to page 3 in the Croatian version too. The sentence that's right below -- please go ahead. You wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was -- I was just wanting to be quite sure that we were talking about the same document. This document, is it letter from Viktor Andreev to -- to me. But I thought that it was -- it's on the 21st of August. Maybe there's some confusion about the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, you may be right, in fact, but could you please look at the document in English. You could see that on the first page it says "From Thornberry," and then on page 2 it says: "From -- from -- from Andreev." Yes. But if you look at the document, I'm sure that you will be able to recall it probably. This is entitled the summary of political issues or political situation, and if you can perhaps just tell us who did this summary or overview of the political situation. The passage that pertains to my question, that's on page 3 where it says the area under the control of the BH Presidency. It says here: "While the BH delegation was in Geneva, Sarajevo has been left in the hands of hardline vice-president Ganic. All the time he has been increasingly aligning himself with the military commanders who talk of fighting on even if there is a settlement in Geneva, in order to achieve the goal of uniting BH." So the impressions that you shared with us about him, do they correspond with those presented in the report that you presented about Mr. Andreev and that you then forwarded to other addressees? Does that reflect your impressions, at least in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As I follow the questioning, I'm remembering my direct examination yesterday and how it was limited by the scope of the Trial Chamber's ruling on which basis this witness was asked to come testify originally as a 92 bis witness as to matters for which we'd indicated other witnesses had testified. The Trial Chamber again indicated others had testified in corroboration of the relevant issues but that it wanted to hear this witness on these issues. There are clearly a good many reports that came to this witness or which this witness sent on to others which were available to the Prosecution which were not led in direct because we tried to limit ourselves to the scope laid down by the Trial Chamber, and I don't think that counsel now is -- is doing the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me remind Defence counsel that initially we had been seized of a 92 bis motion, and the witness statement could have been admitted because a number of testimonies had already been heard on that point. To entitle Defence to put question on Mostar and on another very specific points, we decided that Defence counsel could examine -- cross-examine this witness on very particular points, but now with the questions you're putting, you are addressing other issues. Either you have no questions to put concerning Mostar and in order to use your -- up your time you are addressing issues we have already seen. This is why Mr. Stringer is standing up and objecting. What do you have to say to that, Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe, and I may have misinterpreted this, that the last question -- only the last question that pertains to Mr. Ganic, is indeed related to the issue of Mostar to a great extent. And let me remind Your Honours that this has to do with the witness who testified before this one here in court. So this is why I believe that this is a significant issue. And let me just say that I decided to ask this question precisely on the basis of the part of the statement made by this witness where he indicated the names of the persons that he met, and that is why I asked him whether he knew anything about the person that he received reports about. If, Your Honours, you believe that this is not relevant, the witness has already in part answered my question, and I don't have any other questions in this regard. In fact, I have no further questions for this witness, and this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Ms. Nozica. So your cross-examination has come to an end. It might be better to have our 20-minute break now, and then we will resume our hearing and hear the cross-examination of another Defence counsel. We are now having a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I'd like to give the floor to the next Defence counsel. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Witness, and everybody in the courtroom. Just one note. We've switched with the General Praljak's Defence just so that we're all clear that General Praljak's Defence will be cross-examining this witness too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Thornberry, my name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and in this trial I'm representing General Milivoj Petkovic. I would like to ask you to clarify some details from your statement, and we will also be using some documents to see to what extent -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't sure whether we had finished the lady's comments on Mr. Ganic. Did you want me to complete what I was saying about Mr. Ganic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like to add something to your answer? Please do so if you wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do know Mr. Ganic. I've known him for a number of years, and he is vice-president and has a very wide range of contacts, shall we say, and -- and is a very consummate politician, I would say. That's all, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, in your statement, in paragraph 54 -- or, rather, 56, I apologise, you said that you visited East Mostar, and then you went on to visit West Mostar, and then you said, let me quote -- could you please listen to what I'm saying. I don't think that it will be necessary for you to look at it, but if you want, please do so. This is a document in the Prosecutor binder, and the number is P 10041. The sentence that I'm interested in reads as follows: "We then went to see the HVO in Mostar where they continued the attacks on the UN."

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm really at a loss. I cannot figure out which paragraph the witness [sic] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's in this binder, the Prosecution binder

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 56.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've got the paragraph now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So in paragraph 56 -- let me assist you. It is in the bottom half of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You found it. Okay. So the sentence that I would like you to you to clarify reads as follows. I understand you to be saying that the HVO continued with its attacks on the UN. Did I understand your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I still can't be sure that the paragraph that I am looking at is the one from which the witness [sic] is quoting. I have a paragraph that begins 56: "In mid-August I passed through Split and was approached by my own staff," et cetera. Would that be the same paragraph from which the witness [sic] is commenting?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the paragraph I'm talking about. Now, could you please look at the middle of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think it's line 8, so you say: "We then went to see the HVO in Mostar where they continued the attacks on the UN." Could you please tell us first whether this is what you actually meant to say, that the HVO continued with its attacks on the UN? Are we talking about the HVO attacks?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I simply cannot find this sentence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is -- in the translation there is a little difference. The sentence does not say that they continued to attack but that they proceeded to attack, and it is not necessarily the same meaning. It may be something quite different, and it may be also a verbal attack. I do not know, but maybe it is easy now to -- it's really line 8 from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, thank you. I've got it now. I understand that there are slight differences between the translation and the original. I have this sentence, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So my question was: What HVO attacks on the UN are we talking about here? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: " ... they proceeded to attack the UN," are the words that I understand, and that of course refers to verbal harassment or haranguing, and it might say Mostar where they proceeded verbally to attack the United Nations. That would be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's us assume that these were really verbal attacks, if we assume that. Could you please explain to us who it was in the HVO that verbally attacked the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid I could not. I have no memory of this -- of this particular section of this particular paragraph. I'm sorry. I wish it were different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. We will now skip two sentences, and let us look at the sentence that is -- that starts in the fourth line from the bottom in the same paragraph. I will read it in English so that we may avoid differences in translation. [In English] "Although the HVO officials we met with did not say this directly, the gist of their response was that they would kill us if we attempted to enter East Mostar." [Interpretation] Mr. Thornberry, could you tell us whether this means that the HVO would kill those who entered East Mostar, or is the meaning of it different?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we -- as I seem to remember, we discussed this sentence yesterday, and I was at pains to emphasise that it was a -- a rather gross oversimplification of perhaps a rather complicated idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, could you please tell us whether this sentence actually means that the HVO would kill those who went to East Mostar or the BH army, regardless of whether this was an exaggeration or not?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a gross exaggeration. Well, I don't -- I may say I don't have memory of this sentence, but -- of this paragraph, but earlier in the paragraph it refers to HVO personnel, and it seems to be the case that that sentence or that paragraph is continuing over the next two or three lines so that what the sentence appears to say is that -- that the Bosnian Croats threatened us, and if this -- if we attempted to enter East Mostar. I emphasised yesterday just for our memory's sake that I said that this was a serious overstatement and that the sentence was an exaggeration, an exaggeration from the standpoint of -- of attributing actions and threats without there being any justification for such behaviour. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let us move on, and I believe that we will be able to clarify the relationship of the HVO towards UNPROFOR and the convoy heading for East Mostar later. Mr. Thornberry, you told us that East Mostar was for a time under siege; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor yesterday, you don't have to go looking for it, and let me just state for the record that this is document P 03858, this is a press release by Shannon Boyd, the date is the 21st of August, 1993, and in this document it says -- Mr. Thornberry, please just listen to me carefully. It will be sufficient for you to understand my question. You don't have to do anything else. And it says in this document Commander Budakovic said that the Presidency would agree with the cease-fire but that they have to maintain the corridor towards Jablanica. Budakovic who is mentioned here is a commander of the BH army. The Presidency that is mentioned here is the Muslim civilian government in East Mostar. And my question to you is as follows: Were you aware of the existence the corridor linking Mostar and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if you proceed to ask me what does it -- what -- what was carried along that corridor I might have some difficulty, because I remember being told, and this was something which had to be incorporated from any agreement. The agreement, if it was to have an adequate support on all sides, it would have to take that particular corridor into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to the corridor and discuss it in greater detail on the basis of some documents in due course, but I'd just like now to ask you to clarify part of this statement that I quoted, and from the statement it would emerge that the command of the BH army in Mostar in fact conditioned the cease-fire and humanitarian aid to Mostar with a military element, that is to say by maintaining the corridor towards Jablanica. Those were his conditions. Now, my question to is this: Were you aware of, did you know that the BH army commanders primarily wanted to achieve some military goals even at the expense [Realtime transcript read in error "extent"] of a humanitarian catastrophe in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say, madam, that that was the impression which all of the gentlemen left with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you, and may I have the usher's assistance, please, in helping the witness out, to take a look at document 4D - in my set of documents - 4D 770. It's a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I draw attention to a line in line 37.2 in the transcript. It is said "even at the extent of a humanitarian catastrophe," I think was the word, "in East Mostar." But I think it's not "at the extent" but "at the expense" that you were asking, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that she said "expense."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The interpreters have put it right. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was my question, that certain military goals were reached at the expense of the humanitarian situation in Mostar. So I thank Judge Trechsel for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Thornberry, look at the next document, please, which I would like you to comment, and I'd like us to take a look at the third paragraph from the bottom. At the end of that document, the third paragraph from the bottom where Sulejman Budakovic, writing to his superior, Rasim Delic, says, and I quote: "It would also be good if a helicopter could be found to bring us the approved mortar shells (648 pieces from Krupa) to Glogova which is halfway between Jablanica and Mostar (on the road that our convoy carrying materiel and technical equipment is travelling)." Now, this sentence, Mr. Thornberry, indicates to us that the BH army had this route between Jablanica and Mostar for convoys carrying materiel and technical equipment, MTS. Now, tell us, were you aware of the fact that that particular corridor running from Jablanica to Mostar is one that the BH army used to bring in weapons and other materiel and technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, how would you comment on the following situation on the assumption that it is correct: There's a corridor. It is the Jablanica-Mostar corridor, and the BH army uses that corridor to bring in tonnes, or perhaps that's an exaggeration, hundreds of kilogrammes of materiel and technical equipment, and at the same time that same corridor is not being used to bring in food and other necessities for the life of the population in East Mostar. Now, what would be your comments to that situation on the assumption that it is a correct rendition of the situation?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, they would be adverse comments, and beyond that I could not go unless I had a lot more information available to me. This was a very hot route, as counsel will be aware, and it was going to have to be tidied up before it became in any effective way a corridor for bringing in humanitarian elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say by that that there was no impediment to bringing in hundreds of thousands of materiel and technical equipment, military equipment, but that that same corridor would not be suitable for bringing in food? Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wanted to say what I did say, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I must admit that I didn't understand you fully, but let's move on. Now, look at that same document, please --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: By Sulejman Budakovic and the date is the 25th, 26th of August, 1993. Can you tell us where you were at that time on that day?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I'm just looking for that date. 25, 26 August. I would need to research a little bit in order to identify that. It looks to me as if it was a date -- it was certainly a date within which the discussions and consultations and arguments were taking place about the use of that corridor, amongst others, the use of that corridor for bringing in foodstuffs and -- and medicaments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Mr. Thornberry, that at that time you were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, dear. No, I'm sorry. I would like to agree it, subject to our discussion, but I don't know where my information on that is currently at this time. I would have to -- I would have to take a little bit of time to look within the archives or within the papers available now today before I could actually go ahead and agree -- and agree on that matter. I'm sorry that it's so difficult for me to answer your questions, but a number of these questions go into areas which it's very difficult for me to recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. That is the time that you mention in your statement as the time when the convoy entered East Mostar, and we know from your statement that that is indeed the time that you were there. However, it's not essential that you remember that at the present time. We can establish that on the basis of the documents. I'd like to draw your attention to one more fact now, something that you mention -- well, an assertion you made in actual fact, not a fact. There was mention about the difficult situation for civilians in East Mostar. I'm sure you will remember that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now part of the testimony of a witness, it was a protected witness, so I'm not going to mention the name, but for the record and for anybody who wishes to check it out it was Witness BB, and I'm going to quote the testimony. It was on the record, on page 25335. And I'm going quote --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we're going to quote from closed-session testimony, I think we should be in private session to do that, because that testimony is currently confidential under a protective order of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Mrs. Alaburic, should wish to quote Witness BB, I'd like to remind you that this testimony is confidential. So we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for not thinking of that myself, and I thank Mr. Stringer for stepping in. So may we move into closed -- or, rather, private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, my question to you is this: Did you know that there were inhabitants in East Mostar who wished to leave East Mostar but the Muslim authorities in East Mostar didn't let them? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Much of the population wanted to leave East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we then make the following conclusion: That the BH army used the civilians in East Mostar for achieving its military goals?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would have to get better information than I can give on that subject. It's very difficult for me to have an open discussion in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This question is an important question. You have just answered by saying that most of the people in East Mostar wanted to leave East Mostar. That is what you said, but the question put to you by Ms. Alaburic was a broader question. She was asking you whether the Muslim authorities were preventing these people from leaving East Mostar. So were you made aware of this? What do you have to say about it? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, if I may say so, I -- in the -- I think in the third line, I think that I intended to say much of the population in East Mostar rather than the phrase which I think -- I think you said the most. I don't think I ventured as far as "most," but I'm quite willing to be -- for the matter to be clarified. Now, I have to say that I believe that it's quite likely that -- that much of the population would have liked to leave -- to leave East Mostar because conditions there were becoming so really dreadful. Yes, I think that's the answer I want to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. But -- that's your answer, but you haven't answered the question. They wanted to leave. Why couldn't they leave? Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's in the nature of a siege, sir, that it is -- that the population cannot move individually and -- and upon their own personal decisions. And I think that's the situation -- that was the situation at that time, namely that some people -- some people from East Mostar wanted to leave and were not able to leave in part because of prevention by the -- by the -- I'm sorry, I've lost my place in the -- by the -- by the -- by the authorities of the -- of East Mostar, and there were, to my knowledge in any event, a number of different groups within East Mostar who did not agree with everything or even perhaps in some cases with anything which the notional government of East Mostar wanted to impose. It would be very surprising to me if -- if there were not, in fact, splinter groups, groups which are based on different ethnic foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, I'd like to move on to another topic now, the media campaign, and I'd like to remind you that in paragraph 59 of your statement - you needn't look for it - you said that the tactics of taking TV crews with you in this case proved to be very successful. Now, I'd like to show you a document, once again compiled by Sulejman Budakovic, about the media campaign, so let's take a look at it together. It is 4D 00722.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the usher's help, please, in assisting the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this document Sulejman Budakovic refers to a meeting with you, you needn't worry about the spelling of your name. Now, in certain parts of the former Yugoslavia names were phonetically transcribed as they were pronounced, but I'm interested in the last portion where Sulejman Budakovic says that "Except for media presentation of Mr. Cedric Thornberry and a donation of 300 kilogrammes of medicines, nothing specific was done to help the hungry citizens of Mostar and the surrounding areas. Now, the media campaigns is what we're discussing, and I would like to ask you the following, Mr. Thornberry: Did you have any experience in organising media campaigns, and did you know how in media terms, a problem should be presented for the public to become aware of the problem to the greatest possible extent, to raise public awareness of a problem?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've had several experiences in that field, most notably in Namibia at around the same time as this. In Namibia to a very large degree the success of the campaign was based upon a high level of coverage of electronic and ordinary coverage. We had tried to organise a campaign in --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I do apologise for interrupting you. However, I'd like us to discuss the campaign in greater detail device for East Mostar, not focusing on Namibia. I apologise for that, but tell me whether the purpose of this media campaign, the one we're discussing now, the East Mostar campaign, to have the world public see the difficult situation in East Mostar, to portray the difficult situation in East Mostar, was that the purpose of the campaign?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would recollect that the purpose of the campaign was to shake some of the media and indeed even some of the public authorities elsewhere in the world. My desire -- our intent was to -- to make that campaign more effective perhaps by bringing home to the Western world's and other groups, I may say, not only the Western world, but was to try to bring home to other peoples in the world the -- the dreadful conditions in that country. So, yes, the answer is the main purpose of that campaign was to bring home, to shake from their complacency a large number of people who normally one would have expected would be operating in -- not only in a public relations but in a practical way to help relieve the population of this city.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now tell us, please, the following: Can you -- would you agree with me that a media campaign can be effective if in a simple and well-devised way indicates the problem? So it has to be striking.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends who's going to be struck. I mean, you could have a target audience.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this case specific as you've said, and as we've seen on the basis of a number of documents, the targeted audience was the population of the Western countries, which was supposed to exert influence on the government of its country, to take more energetic measures in resolving the problem in Mostar. Can we agree that that was the object of the campaign?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put it much more succinctly than I did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can we agree then that if we wish to achieve that goal in our media campaign that the message we send out to the public must be simple, easily understood, and convincing?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That helps too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, if in a media campaign you wish to indicate the difficult situation of the Muslim population in East Mostar, for instance, would you in that case indicate the fact that the Muslim authorities do not wish to use the possibility of bringing in food to that part of Mostar or that the Muslim authorities do not wish to reduce the number of inhabitants in East Mostar and thereby make the situation easier for the rest of the population, or would you keep quiet in that media campaign about circumstances like that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I would follow the cogent advice which you had just given us. I agree with it. It is a very good idea to have simple and striking images to bring home. We think that the various media groups which came there with us were actually doing that. They were -- that was their -- that was their task. Many of them were highly professional and practical-minded media people, and basically I think the best thing we could do was to stand aside and -- and let them get on with the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that answer. Now, can we just clarify something else while we're on this subject? Can we agree, you and I, that some political conclusions based on -- or an attempt to establish the facts on the basis of what was contained in a media campaign, that there's great probability that those conclusions will not be correct, or, rather, that they will be incomplete, that most probably they would be over-simplified?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a constant problem in running a media campaign, that not only may it hit to the wrong -- hit the wrong targets and hit them with weapons or -- I mean with darts, with means, it's -- it's important to -- as we've already agreed, it's important to have a thoroughly professional and well-targeted campaign. I'm sorry, I'm perhaps losing you in translation at the moment, but I'm a little puzzled. I'm trying to find a way of communicating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the media campaign, as I can see in paragraph 59, that you did address this issue, and you confirmed, because you told Defence counsel that you felt it was useful to have the media play a part by inviting them to come when you toured the country. So, for instance, when you went and visited the hospital in East Mostar, we've seen the video footage, and C -- CNN media crew came along with you, and we can see, for instance, a child suffering on a hospital bed. Of course this will have a huge impact, but you were neutral, and this was a part you were playing because you were a UN civil servant. Why didn't you ask CNN to come to the hospital in West Mostar so that they could also show a small child in that hospital also who was being treated there? So how did you take your decisions? Why did you decide to have the media come along with you in one place and not another against the backdrop of your objectivity, which should be the golden rule when you have such a mission to carry out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When objectivity, however, turns into passivity, we have a problem, and one of the reasons why we found ourselves in the invidious position of trying to -- to preclude some of the barbarity which was still being practised, I think that we were based to some extent -- our actions were based to some extent by information which was already coming to us when we went into East Mostar. The situation, sir, which I might very briefly mention was one in which the -- the campaign which has been referred to, was a rather blunt instrument. It -- it -- it hit rather bluntly, but it's very difficult, sir, or we found it very difficult some years ago to -- to impact upon a very broad population. That was what we attempted to do. I think we were actually remarkably successful, and not all UN campaigns, information campaigns, have been so successful. But I am absolutely available, sir, should you be more precise about the aspects of the campaign which -- which you feel were lacking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you decided to ask a television crew to come along with you, was this a personal initiative, or were you obeying orders from the top inside the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid that -- I'm afraid that at that time, sir, we were the top. Nobody else was much interested in what was happening in Mostar. That's the blunt truth, I'm afraid. And, sir, I would like just to defend the impartiality of the United Nations. It doesn't mean neutrality. Not to my understanding, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. We have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Still insisting a little bit on this aspect. It does appear that -- that your campaign was a unilateral campaign which in a way took sides and put the blame on one of -- of two parties. Was that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I wouldn't -- I wouldn't -- first of all, it's a long time ago, and my memory is no better than that of someone of my age, but I don't think that our approach to this was unilateral. We operated locally through the local authorities, whoever they might have been, and we've had a discussion on that subject. But also, we sought -- while we were there in Mostar on the first of our visits, we tried to gather as much information as we could. We had public information people with us, and I don't think that our -- our campaign was as sophisticated as it might have been in the sense of targeting an area which was, if I may say, was very well-explored by counsel. So I don't -- I don't really see how we could get a more precisely focused campaign on that first voyage, on that first trip. Later perhaps it might have been said we should have done this or we should have done that, but in the meantime people were being fed. Children were being cared for in hospitals. It is -- it was very easy for outsiders, and some of them did, not many but some of them did, some people were critical of us. They said, "Well, you should have gone through the established channels." The established channels had existed since time began and there was still the edge of famine in that city. I don't myself see the -- I'm the first person to concede that we may have got something wrong, but I don't think we got something wrong, and certainly the media didn't think so. I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, since I believe that I know a thing or two about the media, I would say -- I would agree with you that this was a good media campaign, and I'm not trying to challenge it either from the point of view of the legitimacy of the objective or anything. What I'm interested in is a legal issue, and because you're lawyer, I believe that we will be able to come to an agreement. If we are trying to determine facts relevant to a criminal -- to the criminal proceedings as lawyers, then we will not be relying on the products of a media campaign. Can we agree on that in principle?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily, madam, because you may have a campaign which would develop its own momentum and in that form, in other words a strengthened form, become more effective. I think you perhaps, madam, would accept that there can be. This is a -- a campaign which -- which rolls forward, you hope, not backwards. But -- yeah, sorry, stop, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, we could discuss this topic, which is one of the most interesting topics in law as far as I'm concerned, for a long time, but we have to deal with other topics. In paragraph 69 of your paragraph you're talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm told that you've had your 40 minutes. How much time have other Defence counsel given you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I have been ceded the time that was allotted to Mr. Pusic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just while we're having this brief intervention, I have some news about the next witness that I'd like to share with the Trial Chamber and counsel at some time before we break today, which might affect our scheduling for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you can let us know when we finish. We shall finish with this witness at half past 5.00 because he needs to have a rest. So you will let us know after that. All right? So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, in paragraph 69 we have this very brief sentence. I'm going to read it. You don't have to look for it. You talk about the shelling, and you say: "[In English] It was my impression that the civilians themselves were just as much a target of attack as the military." [Interpretation] I would like to know what facts is this impression of yours based.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information made to us locally by the local authorities, by what we had learned from our military information people before, during, and after our visit to Mostar. I'm sure you know what I mean by that. And I think those are the two main sources, but some governments also provided us with information which has -- which turned out to be extremely accurate, in my opinion, and which was based on the principle of self-defence. Article 51.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say the local government, do you mean the Muslim local government?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, was there another one which was functioning in that area? I only ask because I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, you may have gotten this information from the Croatian government or authorities in West Mostar. That's why I wanted to clarify this point. Mr. Thornberry, could you please tell me, did you know how many BH army units were deployed in East Mostar area and how many troops did the BH army have in that part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I could not answer the question. I didn't have the data now, and I didn't have it then, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, did the local authorities, Muslim or otherwise, give you the information that the BH army often set up artillery weapons close to the hospital that you visited or close to mosques or some other buildings where relatively large quantities of civilians would gather? Did you ever get this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We acquired quite a lot of such information, yes. Maybe you would like to elaborate on your -- on your question, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm quite happy with your answer, because in UNPROFOR documents we did find a number of warnings to the effect that the BH army was setting up its artillery weapons close to such locations.
