And in this regard, I would like to ask you the following: We heard an analysis in this courtroom provided to us by a Prosecution expert about the shelling of Mostar, and among his findings - I'm quoting from memory now - was that about 75 per cent -- or, rather, three-quarters of the casualties in East Mostar were men of military age. Were you aware of this information or information of this sort or to that effect?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly heard from officials and professionals in that area, I mean by that doctors and consultants, specialists, surgeons, what their findings were. I'm sure I could -- if it was necessary, I'm sure I could find that information, or nearly sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you moved around East Mostar, so this is an important question. As far as you're concerned, did you see with your own eyes armed soldiers of the ABiH in East Mostar? With your own eyes, I mean, not what X, Y, Z would have told you. Did you personally with your own eyes see any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, sir. I have to say that because I cannot be at this distance so sure as to be able to say with absolute precision, to answer that question with absolute precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that you think you remember having seen soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me go back to the hospital. We heard witnesses here, and they talked about that hospital that you know, and they said that next to the hospital there were ABiH mortar shells and that they were hitting HVO positions. You see how the whole thing was going on? There were mortars next to the hospital, and those mortars are used to shoot. The HVO, which is the target of the shells, is reacting. Do you think that's quite an extraordinary situation? Is this a realistic description of what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is -- is it an accurate description of what happened? I'm sorry, I didn't -- I missed a part of your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I want to know if the situation as described by some witnesses, and given what you were in a position to witness, is the situation possible? Was it possible for the ABiH, from the hospital in East Mostar, to target the HVO knowing that the HVO will shoot back and that this would cause damage either to the hospital, either among the people who would be killed next to the hospital, and of course knowing that the media will portray the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I know how to answer this question. In every peacekeeping operation that I have had participation, including those of the Middle East, allegations have centred on such allegations as these. Similarly with the use of troops as storm-troopers basically. I don't remember having seen these events. In part, at least, my answer would be based upon some of the reliable sources that I can identify, I think I can identify, and those sources which included also the Spanish authorities were available to me. I don't know whether they were accurate. I do know that they're likely to be much more accurate than we are now today sitting here. But it's very hard, sir, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't see anything. You didn't see mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I did. Oh, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did see mortars next to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I didn't say that I had seen them close to the hospital. I did say that I had seen mortars in the -- in that part of the city, in eastern -- on the eastern side of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, I would like us to move on to a different topic now. It has to do with paragraph 55 of your statement where you say that it was considered to be undoubted that the Bosnian Croats were trying to cut off a part -- to carve off a part of Bosnia for themselves. I would like to ask you a couple of questions about that. Were you aware of the fact that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan from January 1993 envisaged that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be set up as a state comprising ten provinces and that three of the ten provinces were supposed to be so-called Croat provinces? So were you aware of that plan?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course they were not only based on -- on the idea of ten provinces, but they were also based upon the agreement of the parties. What wasn't particularly agreed was when the parties simply started hitting each other on the head with clubs. That wasn't part of Vance-Owen. That was a trial of strength, and that was what from about the end of July onwards, really until Dayton, really what we saw. And I think in a way it's -- I -- I wouldn't want to emphasise this too -- too strongly, I don't think so, but you didn't have to dig very far to find exactly what was going on politically, and those politics were tending to impact upon the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in at this time is whether you were aware that the representatives of Bosnian Croats, as early as in January 1993, accepted the plan that was put on the table.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Accepted until next time it became necessary to find some other alternative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the end of our conversation today we will find out what led to the search for other alternatives, but you can take my word for it now that the representatives of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina signed all the elements of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan from January 1993. Let us now assume that this is indeed so. Can we then conclude that in January 1993 it was not doubtful at all that Croats saw their future within the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state in which Croats would have their own entity, a composite state?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, madam, would you agree that at most -- during most parts of 1993 the weakest militarily body was in fact that corresponding to the HVO? I ask this because I think it is almost -- perhaps almost universally held that the Croats and the Croatian authorities were in a -- in a worse condition militarily, in terms of strength, and that those circumstances, and it -- and it could be said that much of the Croatian concern was to safeguard what they hoped had been agreed, what had been established during the various bilateral and multi-lateral talks which were going on at that time, which were going on frequently at that time. I understand that -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with you, and perhaps we could reformulate this conclusion. Please listen to me and tell me whether we can agree that the representatives of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, as early as in January 1993, wanted to find a peaceful solution to the problems and that they were happy with what the Vance-Owen Peace Plan envisaged for them?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with that, especially as I knew -- I knew that talks were taking place between Muslim and HVO authorities on a fairly frequent basis and had been doing so since -- since about January, February of that time. This inevitably -- must inevitably have an impact upon the strategy and the overall game plan of one of the sides in a -- in a terribly wrought situation as we have been describing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, I prepared two documents for you, but because we don't have enough time let me just refer Their Honours to them, to those documents, and then I will ask you some questions about it. Witness, you don't have to look for this document. I will not be asking you about any details. That's 4D 325. This is the Izetbegovic-Krajisnik agreement signed on the 16th of September, 1993, in particular paragraph 5 envisaging that the referendum should be called on whether the Muslim or the Serbian state should remain within the union of the Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time -- or, rather, two days earlier, and this is document P 0 -- P 50 -- P 051. Presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic signed a document which was almost identical in its contents, but paragraph 5 was quite different. There is no mention of the secession of any part of the territory of the Croatian part of the territory. This document is P 5051. Mr. Thornberry, could you please listen to my question. Sir, you don't have to look at those documents. The Judges will check and see for themselves whether what I'm saying is correct. If Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina in mid --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: If Muslims and Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- in mid-September 1993 are talking about the possibility that a referendum might be called for the Serbian republic to remain within this state and Croats and Muslims do not mention that in their agreement, which is otherwise almost completely identical, can we agree then that Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina felt that both the Croat and the Muslim entities should remain within Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they had no doubts in their minds as to that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really feel that this issue is -- takes place way up high beyond my pay grade. These were the essence of what a lot of the negotiations that were taking place centred upon, and I think you know that as well as I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I hope that Their Honours and my conclusion will be found to be the only logical one. Now, can we move on to a document that I'd like you to look at in my set of documents. It is P 7548.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P 7548. Yes. And I'd like us to focus on paragraph 7. In paragraph 7 of this document -- or, rather, let's define what the document is to begin with. What is the document? Are you familiar with it? Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the "Secretary-General only." That's the next to the highest level of confidentiality which the United Nations uses for its communications. So it --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the document is being sent by Thorvald Stoltenberg. It says from Thorvald Stoltenberg on the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, special representative of the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's right. Now, in point 7 we have a summary of the positions of the three warring parties or conflicting parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You raised a question in my mind. You say that the Secretary-General is next to the highest level of confidentiality. What's the highest level then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most immediate. Most immediate plus in turn ask Mr. Akashi. So it has "most immediate" and Secretary-General only, and that is definitely above my pay grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for the interruption, Mr. President. I'm just looking at this document on my list and it appears to be one that we've marked as under seal. I don't -- I can't say a hundred per cent on that, but could I ask maybe to be cautious, or -- out of -- to have caution just to treat it as such until I can get that confirmed?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing against that. There weren't any markings on the document, so I didn't check, didn't feel that was necessary, but, yes, we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's then move into private session just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the document that I mentioned is the transcript -- or, rather, tape recording from the 235th session the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 14th of January, 1994. The tape recording and transcript is an interesting example of a political action which boils down to the following: How not to accept an agreement which is being proposed by the international community but how to leave the impression that you are willing to cooperate on an international level. Unfortunately, Mr. Thornberry, we're not going to have enough time to deal with the very interesting portions of this transcript, but with regard to this 33 per cent of territory that the Serbs agree should be given over to the Muslims, what Alija Izetbegovic has to say about that, and you will be able to find the translation of that portion on pages 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 19 and 20. Otherwise, the pages are numbered -- well, may we have the usher's assistance, please. The document is 4D 930, and the part that I'd like to refer to is to be found on pages 19 and 20. It is the statement by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, pages 19 and 20. Alija Izetbegovic is speaking. Witness, you might hear a different interpretation to the written text, but that is because different translators and interpreters are working. I think it is an important portion. It's not -- I don't usually read the document, but I think that it will be important for me to do so. Alija Izetbegovic says as followings and I quote: "Let us understand, all these talks we had including the republics and the 33 per cent, et cetera, none of that has been determined, because Klaus warned me," and I think it was Klaus Kinkel that he was referring to, "they" -- I apologise. I won't think any more. I've been put right. "Klaus warned me when I talked about some things he said, you know, Mr. Izetbegovic, the rule about politics. Until we agree on everything, we agree on nothing. So so far we have not agreed on anything. These are all just pre-conditions for some agreement. "Of course we can, if it suits us, go back to the beginning. We only have to ask ourselves if we have a better solution. But as soon as we see that we're better off, then turn everything back to the beginning."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before there's a question, I just want to raise an objection again to taking the witness to this document which I don't think any of us have ever seen before. It's -- it purports to be from January 1994, which is after this witness's time in Mostar certainly, which was again the reason, primary reason for his being asked to come testify. I've said it before. I'm going say it again. There are lots of interesting things that I could have led from this witness on my direct which I didn't because of the limitations, and I think that this is unfair at this point to go as far down this road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two issues here, Ms. Alaburic. Limitations on the cross-examination do not entitle you to address this issue, all the more that as Mr. Stringer has said, this is a document that's dated January 1994, and the witness was no longer operating in that area in Mostar. So needless to spend any time on that. Just ask your question briefly, because we need to have a break now. So put the question you wanted to highlight.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be allowed to respond to Mr. Stringer. My question follows on from part of the witness's statement contained in paragraph 55 to the effect that it was the Croats that tried to cut off part of Bosnia for themselves. That's why I ask about the Vance-Owen Plan. That's where my question about the Krajisnik-Izetbegovic agreement or Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreements comes from, and that is why I'm working up slowing to this transcript. It is true that the transcript is from 1994 but Alija Izetbegovic speaks of his own policy from the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and so therefore what he says there has to do with January 1993 as well as well as the whole of 1993. So it does refer to the relevant time, the time relevant in the indictment. I consider this to be an extremely important transcript. I've had it for a long time but not used it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will read the minutes right through.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I be allowed to summarise? In continuation Alija Izetbegovic goes on to say that the army of Republika Srpska was too strong for the BH army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mrs. Alaburic, no. Please put your question. You -- there's a document that states such-and-such and then you put your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- yes, that's precisely what I want to say, what it says in the document, because if I go on to ask my question without laying the foundations, then the objection is raised that I have not laid the foundations for my question. So that is why I wish to say what it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to adjourn now. You have had approximately 70 minutes, 40 minutes which was your own time, the Pusic Defence gave you the rest. So theoretically you have ten minutes left for tomorrow. So please do your calculations again. Sir, we shall meet again tomorrow at 2.15 p.m., because the hearing will be in the afternoon tomorrow. So may I ask you to follow the usher, because Mr. Stringer needs to take the floor on another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, do you wish to be heard in closed session or in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Public is fine. Public is okay, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for scheduling tomorrow. While the proceedings have been taking place this afternoon, I've been informed that everything that needed to happen in respect of the next witness has already happened. He is ready to testify, and he can testify tomorrow if the schedule allows, and that he has informed our people now that he is not seeking any protective measures so that he can testify in open session. So that's the news for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this piece of information. Theoretically tomorrow Ms. Alaburic still has ten minutes left for her cross-examination. Then we will hear Mr. Praljak's Defence, who I believe will use his 40 minutes, and I think Coric's Defence had given their time to somebody else. I don't know if Coric's Defence wishes to take the floor tomorrow. Do you wish to take the floor tomorrow or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: The Defence of Mr. Coric cedes its time to the Petkovic Defence and Mr. Praljak if they need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if we do not lose any time, we will be able to finish with this witness tomorrow and then hear the next witness after that. You have already indicated that this is a 92 ter witness and that you will lead the witness for a short time and the Defence teams will have one hour and 40 minutes approximately. This is what I seem to remember. So we shall meet again tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
